citations.review_text:
Before you play: get the mikiri counter in the skill tree, it'll make bosses that seem impossible much easier.

Dark souls but more parry based and generally focused on having the player learn patterns and adapt through its more rhythmic parrying combat. The stealth is also pretty neat and the bosses are in my opinion extremely fun. The game is also quite linear i guess, but do note that you need a decently performing PC to play this game (RIP my GPU, i use an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1050 Ti and can barely run the game on the lowest possible graphics). Overall, if stealth, linear progression, challenging yet fun trial and error esque bosses, parry based combat, and a pretty good story to go with it interest you and you have the specs to atleast run it on low graphics (otherwise you'd have to mod the game and further decrease graphics) then go ahead. Still though, if you really dont like hard games, i wouldn't really recommend the game.

FromSoftware takes a different direction with Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, replacing the familiar RPG progression of Dark Souls and Bloodborne with a focused experience built around precision, discipline and mastery. Set in a fictionalized interpretation of Japan's Sengoku period, Sekiro blends historical atmosphere, Japanese mythology, religious symbolism and supernatural horror into one of the studio's most distinctive creations.
Combat: A Test of Discipline and Mastery
Sekiro's greatest achievement is its combat system. Deflection, posture and precise timing transform sword fighting into an intense exchange of pressure and anticipation. Rather than relying on character builds or increasingly powerful equipment, success depends on understanding enemy patterns, mastering timing and maintaining composure.

The prosthetic arm, with its shurikens, firecrackers, axes and other tools, introduces tactical variety, while stealth and the grappling hook reinforce the freedom of movement expected from a shinobi. Progression feels genuinely earned: you do not simply become stronger; you become a better swordsman.
Exploration and World Design: Historical Japan Meets the Supernatural
Initially grounded in the Sengoku period, Ashina gradually reveals a much stranger world beneath its historical exterior. From Ashina Castle and the mist-covered Ashina Depths to the unsettling Mibu Village and the ethereal Fountainhead Palace, every location contributes to an atmosphere that balances beauty, mystery and decay.

The transition into the supernatural is particularly effective. The Fountainhead Palace, with its sacred architecture, vibrant vegetation and divine inhabitants, feels like an entirely different plane of existence.
Japanese Mythology and Religious Philosophy

Stop dodging. This isn't Dark Souls—it's a high-stakes rhythm game with katanas.

You can't over-level your stats or summon help to bail you out here. You either learn to parry, hit your Mikiri Counters, and break posture, or you die in two hits. It will humble you for the first ten hours, and then the combat clicks and makes you feel like an untouchable shinobi god.

10/10 hesitation is defeat.

single_points.text: One reviewer says the auto-lock regularly unlocks or fails to lock at will.

citation.review_text:
Overall, I greatly disliked my experience with Sekiro. For context, I played all three Dark Souls games leading up to this: I enjoyed DS1 the most, completed DS2 but did not enjoy it, and dropped DS3. I tried to keep an open mind that this is not like those. But the game has been a chore from the start, and is extremely challenging when it comes to reaction time & pattern recognition! These two things are almost the entire game, and are very much not my main motivator when I chose to play a game.

First, FromSoft continues their streak of clunky controls. I played almost the entire game on a gamepad, and again found myself in many cases where the controls did not behave how expected. Auto-lock remains unfamiliar with the concept of "object permanence" and regularly unlocks or fails to lock at will. Second, certain aspects of the meta gameplay elements are annoying and unnecessary. Sekiro should have auto-loot and losing half my resources on death really only serves to waste time. Third, operating as a 'shinobi' between bosses is a mediocre experience between how the NPCs function and the linearity of the level design. Fourth, there's very limited space for self-expression in the combat. There are some tools that allow variety in the 'overworld' navigation, but otherwise each tool generally has a use case & that's it. Finally, this game's animation, sound, & graphical designs are rather inaccessible or perplexingly unintuitive in regularly interacted systems. For example, a 'thrust' perilous attack is not always the same as a thrusting motion, even though both may have very similar telegraphing by animation. Additionally, there are certain sound queues that are subtle but can be quite important, and the perilous attack markers being different characters but the same color will confuse the heck out of some people.

Despite these grating aspects, the game has a distinct identity where the atmosphere of being a warrior in vaguely feudal Japan could be rather engaging fo…

single_points.text: One reviewer says the controllers are no longer recognized by the game.

citation.review_text:
It was while I could still play it.
I had played this back in 2022/23 with a controller, if I remember correctly, but know I decided to finish it off. Welp, the controllers are no longer recognized from the game even after using every official/3rd party troubleshooting method -- yes, even the "unplug the KB and mouse dongles" method.

Don't get me wrong, the game is AMAZING but this is a dealbreaker for me here.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a steep learning curve and high difficulty at the start before the combat mechanics click.

citations.review_text: Sekiro is, in my opinion, one of the only "Sekiro-likes" you need to play. It laid the groundwork for every game that Geoff Keighley will insist is "a game changer" and will "revolutionize gaming." It has a learning curve for sure, but the game is very satisfying once it clicks. Once you get used to how it plays, every loss feels less like a "damn this is unfair" and more "what do I need to change." You always have the tools you need, so get out there and use them.
Steep learning curve at the start. If you can get past that the game is AMAZING 9/10 would platinum again.
